[[File:Dasiphora fruticosa - põõsasmaran.jpg|thumbnail|''Dasiphora fruticosa'' subsp. ''fruticosa'', Estonia]]

'''''Dasiphora fruticosa''''' is a [[species]] of [[hardiness (plants)|hardy]] [[deciduous]] flowering [[shrub]] in the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Rosaceae]], [[native plant|native]] to the cool [[temperateness|temperate]] and [[subarctic]] regions of the northern hemisphere, often growing at high elevations in mountains. ''Dasiphora fruticosa'' is still widely referenced in the horticultural literature under its synonym '''''Potentilla fruticosa'''''. Common names include '''shrubby cinquefoil''',<ref name=GRIN>{{GRIN | accessdate=3 June 2014}}</ref> '''golden hardhack''',<ref name=GRIN/> '''bush cinquefoil''',<ref name=GRIN/> '''shrubby five-finger''',<ref>{{cite book |author1=Weeks, S.S. |author2=Weeks, H.P. |year=2012  |title=Shrubs and Woody Vines of Indiana and the Midwest: Identification, Wildlife Values, and Landscaping Use |publisher=Purdue University Press  |isbn=9781557536105 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=O-S6uVDWTjoC }}</ref> '''widdy''',<ref name=GRIN/> '''kuril tea'''<ref name="Kuril">{{cite web |title=Kuril Tea |url=https://naturasiberica.ee/en/ingredient/kuril-tea/ |website=Natura Siberica |access-date=17 March 2022}}</ref> and '''tundra rose'''.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Tundra rose |url=https://www.projectnoah.org/spottings/123860020 |access-date=2024-02-19 |website=Project Noah}}</ref>

==Description==
It grows to {{convert|0.1|–|1|m|in|1|abbr=on}} tall, rarely up to {{convert|1.5|m|ft|1|abbr=on}}. The habit is variably upright to sprawling or [[prostrate shrub|prostrate]], but stems are often ascending especially those stems with many long branches. The [[Bark (botany)|bark]] of older stems is shreddy with long thin strips. The plants are densely leafy, the [[leaf|leaves]] divided into five or seven (occasionally three or nine) [[pinnate]] leaflets. The leaflets are linear-oblong, {{convert|3|-|20|mm|in|1|abbr=on}} long, with entire margins and more or less acute ends. The foliage (both leaves and young stems) is pubescent, variably covered in fine silky, silvery hairs about 1 mm long. The [[flower]]s are produced terminally on the stems and are {{convert|2|-|3|cm|in|1|abbr=on}} cm across, [[Ranunculus|buttercup]]-shaped, with five petals and 15–25 stamens; the petals are pale to bright yellow (orange to reddish in some western Chinese populations). The [[fruit]] is a cluster of [[achene]]s covered with long hairs. The species is variably [[plant sexuality|dioecious]] or [[plant sexuality|bisexual]]; flowering is typically from early to late summer. It is normally found growing in moisture-retentive soils in swamps and rocky areas.<ref name=fnwe>Flora of NW Europe: [http://ip30.eti.uva.nl/BIS/flora.php?selected=beschrijving&menuentry=soorten&id=2628 ''Potentilla fruticosa''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110717032219/http://ip30.eti.uva.nl/BIS/flora.php?selected=beschrijving&menuentry=soorten&id=2628 |date=2011-07-17 }}</ref><ref name=blamey>Blamey, M. & Grey-Wilson, C. (1989). ''Flora of Britain and Northern Europe''. {{ISBN|0-340-40170-2}}</ref><ref name=china>Flora of China: [http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200011065 ''Potentilla fruticosa'']</ref><ref name=jepson>Jepson Flora of California: [http://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/cgi-bin/get_JM_treatment.pl?Potentilla+fruticosa ''Potentilla fruticosa'']</ref><ref name=bc>Plants of British Columbia: [http://linnet.geog.ubc.ca/Atlas/Atlas.aspx?sciname=Pentaphylloides%20floribunda ''Pentaphylloides fruticosa''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110706210915/http://linnet.geog.ubc.ca/Atlas/Atlas.aspx?sciname=Pentaphylloides%20floribunda |date=2011-07-06 }}</ref><ref name=rhs>Huxley, A, ed. (1992). ''New RHS Dictionary of Gardening'' 3: 697. Macmillan {{ISBN|0-333-47494-5}}.</ref>

The plant is usually only eaten by wildlife when other food sources are scarce,<ref>{{Cite book|last=Reiner|first=Ralph E.|title=Introducing the Flowering Beauty of Glacier National Park and the Majestic High Rockies|publisher=Glacier Park, Inc.|year=1969|pages=50}}</ref>.

*''Dasiphora fruticosa'' subsp. ''fruticosa''. Described from Yorkshire, England and Öland, Sweden.<ref name=L.>Linnaeus, C. (1753). ''Species Plantarum'' 1: 495. [http://www.botanicus.org/title.aspx?bibid=b12069590 Online facsimile (scroll to page 495)]</ref> Northern Europe (scattered, in Estonia, Great Britain, Ireland, Latvia, and Sweden) and northern and central Asia.<ref name=grin1>{{GRIN | ''Dasiphora fruticosa'' subsp. ''fruticosa'' | 450402 | accessdate = 20 December 2017}}</ref>

Described from Canada, New York, and New Jersey, North America.<ref name=pursh>Pursh, F. T. (1813). ''Flora Americae Septentrionalis'' 1: 355-356. [https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/title/b11729004 Online facsimile (scroll to pages 355-356)] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080305065711/http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/title/b11729004 |date=2008-03-05 }}</ref> Asia, southern Europe (Spain east to Bulgaria), and North America.<ref name=bc/><ref name=grin2>{{GRIN | ''Dasiphora fruticosa'' subsp. ''floribunda'' | 450402 | accessdate = 20 December 2017}}</ref><ref>Weber, William. 1976. Rocky Mountain Flora. University Press of Colorado, Niwot.</ref><ref>Carter, Jack. 2006. Trees and Shrubs of Colorado. Mimbres Publishing, New Mexico.</ref>

*[[Dasiphora fruticosa var. veitchii|''Dasiphora fruticosa'' var. ''veitchii'']] <small>(E.H.Wilson) Nakai</small> (syns ''Dasiphora veitchii'' <small>(E.H.Wilson) Soják</small>, ''Potentilla arbuscula'' var. ==Cultivation and decorative uses==
[[File:Dasiphora fruticosa 'Mckay's White' 03.jpg|thumb|'Mckay's White' cultivar]]
Shrubby cinquefoil is a popular [[ornamental plant]] in temperate regions.  Different [[cultivar]]s are variable with flowers ranging from white to yellow, orange and pink, but they are all [[Hardiness (plants)|hardy]] plants that produce flowers for much of the summer. The flowers are always small, flat, and round, but there are many dozens on each bush. It is very often used by cities and businesses for landscaping because of its hardiness and low maintenance. It was introduced into cultivation in the 18th century, but many of the modern cultivars, particularly those with orange or red flowers, derive from collections by [[Reginald Farrer]] in western China in the early 20th century.<ref name=rhs/> The vast majority of sellers and gardeners still use the old name ''Potentilla fruticosa''.

All the characteristics of small leaves, delicate flowers, and orange to brown flaky bark make the shrubby cinquefoil suitable for [[bonsai]]. It is very popular in Japan and is gaining popularity in Europe.<ref name="Ma-Ke_Potentilla fruticosa ">{{cite web | first=Mark | last=D'Cruz | title=Ma-Ke Bonsai Care Guide for Potentilla fruticosa | publisher=Ma-Ke Bonsai | url=http://makebonsai.com/guide/bonsailink.asp?quicklink=5109&name=Potentilla_fruticosa | accessdate=2011-04-19 | archive-date=2012-07-21 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120721081608/http://makebonsai.com/guide/bonsailink.asp?quicklink=5109&name=Potentilla_fruticosa | url-status=dead }}</ref>

*'Chelsea Star' – small yellow flowers. {{smallcaps|agm}}<ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Potentila fruticosa'' 'Chelsea Star'|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/59124/Potentilla-fruticosa-Chelsea-Star/Details | access-date = 17 February 2021}}</ref> 
*'Coronation Triumph' – medium-bright yellow flowers, plants are drought- and cold-tolerant and heavy bloomers.
*'Daydawn' – salmon-pink flowers.<!-- AGM withdrawn{{smallcaps|agm}}-->
